For most of the twentieth century, air conditioning was a luxury concentrated in a handful of wealthy, hot countries, above all the United States. Each new generation of compressors accomplished more cooling per watt, and the electricity devoted to keeping cool remained a modest share of the global total. That reassuring equilibrium has been disrupted by rising incomes in the tropics. Hundreds of millions of families in India, Indonesia, and other warm, populous countries are buying their first units, and every machine switched on during a heat wave adds to the strain on the grid at the very moment demand peaks. A 2018 report by the International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that fans and air conditioners already accounted for about a tenth of global electricity consumption and forecast that the number of units in operation could more than triple by 2050.
The consequences are already conspicuous on the hottest days of the year. Grid operators in several regions, which had planned for steadily rising demand, have reported that summer peaks climbed faster than expected, largely because of the spread of air conditioners. Delhi — to take one example — has repeatedly set records for peak electricity demand during summer heat waves. Manufacturers insist that the trajectory is manageable and that better machines will ultimately ____ the extra demand by using variable-speed compressors, smarter thermostats, and refrigerants that trap far less heat.
Skeptics remain unpersuaded. They observe that efficiency gains have historically been swallowed by rising consumption — a pattern economists call the rebound effect — and that utilities in many regions still meet summer peaks by firing up their dirtiest plants. They also point to a vicious circle: the machines expel heat into city streets and, through leaking refrigerants and fossil-fueled power, warm the very planet that makes them necessary. Whether cooling proves a net burden or a manageable cost for the climate, they contend, depends less on engineering ingenuity than on deliberate choices about how buildings are designed and how their electricity is generated.

When speakers encounter a word whose structure makes no sense to them, they sometimes reshape it into something that seems more transparent — a process linguists call folk etymology. The results can be charming. The Old English word brydguma combined bride with guma — an archaic word for man. As guma fell out of use, speakers no longer recognized it, and by the sixteenth century it had been reinterpreted as groom, which then meant a male servant, so that the bridegroom became, in effect, the bride's attendant. Similarly, shamefaced was originally shamefast, meaning held fast by modesty, in the same sense that steadfast means firmly fixed; once the suffix lost its meaning, speakers substituted the more familiar face.
Borrowings from other languages are especially <u>susceptible</u>. The name of a North American rodent, adapted from an Algonquian word, was refashioned by English settlers into woodchuck, although the animal has nothing to do with chucking wood. The cockroach owes its English form to the Spanish cucaracha, recast as if it were composed of two English words. Even polished speakers participate: asparagus was long called sparrowgrass in England, a form that some eighteenth-century authorities described as the customary pronunciation in polite company.
Folk etymology is often regarded as a species of error, and in a narrow sense it is one, since the new form misrepresents the history of the word. Linguists nonetheless tend to view it sympathetically. It reveals that ordinary speakers are not passive recipients of vocabulary but active interpreters who expect words to mean something. A form that seems arbitrary is a burden on memory, whereas a form that appears to be assembled from familiar parts is easier to learn and recall, even if the parts mislead.
The phenomenon is by no means confined to English. Speakers of every language reinterpret opaque words, and many folk etymologies have become so entrenched that it would be pedantic to call them mistakes. They are simply part of the language now, preserving in their very shape a record of how earlier generations strove to make sense of it.

By the 1840s astronomers had a puzzle on their hands. Uranus (discovered by William Herschel in 1781) stubbornly refused to follow the path that Newton's law of gravitation predicted for it. Its position wavered, now slightly ahead of schedule, now slightly behind, by amounts too large to blame on careless observation. Some scientists wondered whether Newton's law itself (hitherto spectacularly successful) weakened over immense distances. Others suspected a more conventional culprit — an unseen planet lying still farther from the Sun, whose gravity was tugging Uranus off course.
Two mathematicians pursued the second hypothesis independently. In England, John Couch Adams — a young graduate of Cambridge — calculated the probable position of the hypothetical planet, but his results met with a lukewarm reception from senior astronomers, and the search that eventually began at Cambridge was sluggish and fruitless. In France, Urbain Le Verrier performed similar calculations and, unable to persuade observers in Paris to act promptly, sent his prediction to Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory. On the very night Galle received the letter in September 1846, he and his assistant located the planet within about one degree of the predicted spot.
The discovery was hailed as a triumph of theory over mere observation — a world had been found with pen and paper before anyone had knowingly glimpsed it. When I first read the correspondence of the period as a student, what struck me was less the genius of the calculation than the certainty of its authors. The discovery also ignited a rancorous quarrel over credit between British and French scientists — a dispute that historians have revisited many times since. Ironically, the same method later led its champion astray. When the orbit of Mercury displayed a small anomaly of its own, Le Verrier postulated yet another hidden planet, which came to be called Vulcan. No such body exists. The discrepancy was finally explained in 1915 by Einstein's general theory of relativity, which showed that, in this instance, it was ____ that required revision.

"If you rush the glue, the book will remember," Mrs. Ferrante said, lifting the brush out of my hand before I could protest.
I had answered the notice in the window of her narrow shop near the university, expecting to spend the summer shelving and running errands. Instead, on my first morning she handed me a hymnal whose spine had split in three places and told me to take it apart. It took me two days. She made me number every gathering of pages in pencil, cut the old threads one by one, and scrape the brittle glue from the folds with a blunt knife. When I grumbled that a machine could rebind the whole thing in an hour, she agreed. "A machine would also trim the margins," she said, "and lose the notes someone wrote there in 1931."
For weeks I sewed practice books from scrap paper, and for weeks she <u>unpicked</u> them. My stitches were too tight, then too loose; my folds drifted off true by a millimeter that she could detect with a fingertip. She seldom praised anything, but she was never impatient with honest mistakes, only with careless ones, and she distinguished between them with unnerving accuracy.
In August a woman brought in a cookbook so battered that its pages were held together with rubber bands. It had belonged to her mother. Mrs. Ferrante gave it to me. I labored over it for nine days, and when I finally pressed the new cover onto the boards and left it overnight beneath a stack of dictionaries, I could not sleep. The next morning the woman opened it, turned to a page stained with what looked like tomato sauce, and wept. Mrs. Ferrante said nothing to me then. But that afternoon she moved my stool from the corner to the bench beside her own.

The promise of the cashierless store is seductively simple — walk in, pick up what you want, and walk out, while cameras and shelf sensors tally your purchases and charge your account automatically. Amazon opened the first of its Go stores to the public in Seattle in 2018, and the company later licensed the underlying technology (branded Just Walk Out) to stadiums, airports, and university campuses. Competitors in China, Japan, and Korea experimented with their own versions, some relying on radio tags attached to each item rather than on computer vision.
The model has proved harder to scale than its champions anticipated. In 2024 Amazon announced that it would remove Just Walk Out from its large Fresh grocery stores in the United States, replacing it with smart carts that customers scan themselves. Media reports at the time claimed that a large team of workers overseas reviewed many of the transactions by watching video footage; Amazon disputed that characterization, saying the staff chiefly labeled data to improve the system. Whatever the precise division of labor, the episode <u>punctured</u> the impression that the stores operated without human involvement.
In Korea a humbler variant has spread rapidly — small shops selling ice cream, snacks, or stationery, staffed by no one at all and monitored remotely through security cameras. When I visited one such shop late one evening, the only sound was the hum of the freezers. Owners welcome the savings on wages and the ability to remain open around the clock. Yet the arrangement redistributes burdens rather than eliminating them. Shoplifting and vandalism must be dealt with after the fact, often by owners scrutinizing footage late at night, and elderly customers unfamiliar with self-service kiosks may find themselves effectively excluded. The automated store, in other words, does not abolish labor so much as relocate it — to distant reviewers, to anxious proprietors, and to the customers who now perform the cashier's work themselves.

From the late seventeenth century until the early nineteenth, a young Englishman of wealthy family was expected to complete his education with a journey across the Continent that could last from several months to several years. The itinerary of this Grand Tour was fairly standardized. Travelers crossed the Channel to France, lingered in Paris to acquire polished manners and fluent French, and then crossed the Alps, often carried over the mountain passes in chairs Ⓐ<u>borne</u> by local porters, to reach the true objective, Italy. In Rome, Florence, and Venice they studied classical ruins and Renaissance paintings, the remnants of a civilization Ⓑ<u>which</u> they had read about since childhood in Latin grammar lessons.
The young men rarely traveled alone. Most were accompanied by a tutor — often an impecunious scholar or clergyman — whose task was to supervise their studies and restrain their excesses. The task frequently proved impossible. Contemporary satirists ridiculed tourists who returned with affected accents, extravagant clothing, and debts, having spent more time Ⓒ<u>gambled</u> and flirting than contemplating antiquity. Parents nonetheless regarded the expense as a sound investment, since familiarity with Continental culture marked a gentleman as fit for political office and polite society.
The Tour left a durable imprint on British taste. Travelers shipped home crates of sculpture, antiquities, and paintings, many of which still adorn country houses and museums. I have walked through several of those houses, and the souvenirs remain where the travelers' fathers placed them. Demand for souvenirs sustained entire trades — the Venetian painter Canaletto produced views of his city Ⓓ<u>largely</u> for English buyers. The custom waned in the nineteenth century, when railways and steamships made Continental travel cheaper and faster, and the leisurely aristocratic pilgrimage gave way to the organized excursions of an expanding middle class. Some historians regard the Grand Tour as the ancestor of modern tourism, though its participants would have been appalled to hear their education described in such commercial terms.

In 2010 three researchers published a study suggesting that posture could alter not only how confident a person felt but also the chemistry of the body. Participants who spent two minutes in expansive 'power poses' (such as leaning back with their hands clasped behind the head) reportedly showed higher levels of testosterone, lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol, and a greater appetite for risk than participants who adopted cramped, contracted postures. The finding was irresistible — a free and effortless intervention that seemed to promise a measurable advantage before job interviews or examinations. A lecture popularizing the idea became one of the most watched talks ever posted online, and corporate trainers eagerly incorporated the poses into their workshops.
Subsequent scrutiny has been less flattering. In 2015 a team using a considerably larger sample attempted to reproduce the original experiment and found no effect on hormones or on willingness to gamble, although participants did report feeling somewhat more powerful. The following year one of the original authors publicly announced that she no longer believed the effects were real, and she described analytical choices in the initial study that, while common at the time, are now recognized as prone to generating spurious results. Defenders of the research maintain that the modest effect on self-reported feelings is genuine, but even sympathetic reviewers concede that the dramatic physiological claims were ____.
The episode has become a cautionary tale in the broader reckoning that psychologists call the replication crisis. Small samples, flexible analyses, and the predilection of journals for striking positive findings conspired to produce a literature in which many celebrated effects proved fragile. None of this means that posture is irrelevant to how people feel; ordinary experience suggests otherwise. But the saga illustrates how a vivid result can outrun its evidence, acquiring the status of established fact through sheer repetition before anyone has rigorously tested it.

Among the many forms the early novel assumed, one of the most popular was also one of the most artificial — the story told entirely through letters. Samuel Richardson's Pamela (published in 1740) consists almost wholly of the correspondence of a young servant who resists the advances of her employer, and its success inspired a deluge of imitators across Europe. Richardson followed it with Clarissa, a vast epistolary tragedy that remains among the longest novels in the English language, and on the Continent the form reached a pinnacle of sophistication in Choderlos de Laclos's Dangerous Liaisons in 1782.
The appeal of the letter novel lay in its <u>immediacy</u>. Because characters wrote — as Richardson put it — 'to the moment,' readers seemed to witness emotions as they unfolded rather than as they were recollected afterward. A heroine could describe a threat while still uncertain how it would end, and the reader shared her suspense. Letters also allowed authors to juxtapose conflicting perspectives without an intrusive narrator — in Laclos's novel, the same event appears in the triumphant letters of the schemers and the anguished letters of their victims, and the reader must reconcile the versions.
I confess a fondness for the form, but its drawbacks were conspicuous. Critics mocked heroines who continued composing lengthy, elegantly phrased letters in the midst of abductions and fires, and the need to justify why every crucial scene was committed to paper strained credibility. By the early nineteenth century most novelists had abandoned the device in favor of a third-person narrator able to enter the minds of several characters at once. Yet the epistolary impulse never entirely vanished. It resurfaced in Mary Shelley's Frankenstein and Bram Stoker's Dracula, and some critics discern its descendants in contemporary novels assembled from emails, text messages, and social media posts.

Cuttlefish, relatives of squid and octopuses, are among the most accomplished masters of disguise in the sea. Within a fraction of a second they can alter the color, pattern, and even the apparent texture of their skin, blending into sand, rock, or seaweed, or flashing bold stripes to startle a predator or court a mate. [A]
The mechanism lies in the skin. Each animal possesses millions of chromatophores, tiny elastic sacs of yellow, red, or brown pigment, each encircled by muscles controlled directly by nerves from the brain. When the muscles contract, a sac is stretched open and its pigment becomes visible; when they relax, it shrinks to an almost imperceptible dot. Beneath the chromatophores lie reflective cells that produce iridescent blues and greens and a white layer that scatters light. Tiny muscles can also raise bumps called papillae, allowing a smooth animal to mimic the rough surface of coral or a frond of algae. [B]
Experiments have shown that cuttlefish do not replicate their surroundings in detail. Instead, they appear to deploy a limited repertoire of general patterns (uniform, mottled, or disruptive), selecting among them according to visual cues such as the size and contrast of nearby objects. Researchers have tested this by placing the animals on artificial checkerboards — when the squares roughly match the size of a distinctive white patch on the cuttlefish's own body, the animals tend to adopt bold disruptive markings. [C]
The ability poses a profound puzzle. By most measures, cuttlefish are colorblind, since their eyes contain only one type of photoreceptor. How an animal that apparently cannot distinguish hues matches the colors of its background so convincingly remains unresolved. Some researchers have suggested that the peculiar U-shaped pupil may allow the eye to extract color information from the way different wavelengths come into focus, while others have proposed that light-sensitive proteins in the skin itself contribute. [D] Neither hypothesis has yet been confirmed.

Most mathematics teachers have watched the same scene unfold. A student is handed an unfamiliar kind of problem, stares at it, tries one approach after another, and eventually either stumbles on the answer or abandons the attempt in frustration. The traditional view holds that such struggle is valuable — by wrestling with problems on their own, learners discover methods for themselves and retain them better. Research on beginners, however, points in a different direction.
In the 1980s the Australian psychologist John Sweller and his colleagues began investigating what they called cognitive load, the demand that a task places on working memory (which can hold only a handful of new elements at once). A novice confronting an unfamiliar problem must keep in mind the goal, the current state of the problem, and the possible moves between them, a juggling act that leaves little capacity for noticing the underlying principle. Sweller's experiments suggested that beginners often learn more by studying (A) ____ solutions, laid out step by step, before attempting similar problems themselves. Learners who alternated between reading a worked example and solving a parallel problem frequently outperformed those who spent the same time solving problems unaided.
The effect has an important limit. As learners gain expertise, worked examples become redundant and can even impair performance — a phenomenon researchers call the expertise reversal effect. Students who already understand a procedure gain little from reading every step and may be distracted by information they no longer need; for them, independent problem solving is the more productive exercise. The appropriate amount of guidance, in other words, should (B) ____ as competence grows.
Some educators worry that worked examples encourage passive imitation. Researchers respond that examples are most effective when students are prompted to explain each step to themselves, and when support is withdrawn gradually, for instance by omitting the final steps of a solution for the learner to complete. Struggle, on this view, is not worthless; it is simply more fruitful once the learner possesses enough knowledge to struggle productively.

In 1602 the States General of the Dutch Republic granted a charter to the United East India Company (known by its Dutch initials as the VOC), giving it a monopoly on Dutch trade with Asia. The company was a novel kind of institution. Earlier trading ventures had typically been financed voyage by voyage — investors pooled money to fit out a fleet, and when the ships returned, the profits were divided and the partnership dissolved. The VOC, by contrast, raised capital that was committed for years and soon (in practice) <u>indefinitely</u>, allowing it to build warehouses, fortresses, and a permanent fleet.
Because investors could not withdraw their money from the company, they needed another way to recover it. The solution was to let them sell their shares to other investors. Trading in VOC shares soon became a routine activity in Amsterdam, conducted first in the open air and then in a purpose-built exchange completed in 1611. Many historians therefore regard the VOC as one of the first companies whose shares were traded publicly, and Amsterdam as the site of an early stock market, complete with brokers, speculation, and even contracts resembling modern futures and options.
The company's commercial success was spectacular for much of the seventeenth century, and it paid lavish dividends. Yet its power rested on coercion as well as commerce. The charter authorized it to wage war, conclude treaties, and govern territories, and it wielded these powers ruthlessly. In the Banda Islands (then the world's only source of nutmeg), company forces under Jan Pieterszoon Coen killed, enslaved, or expelled most of the inhabitants in 1621 to secure control of the spice.
By the late eighteenth century the VOC was mired in debt, enfeebled by corruption, competition, and war, and it was dissolved in 1799. Its legacy remains ambivalent. The financial innovations it pioneered became foundations of modern capitalism, while its conduct in Asia illustrates how a commercial enterprise armed with state authority could inflict immense suffering.

Artemisia Gentileschi (born in Rome in 1593) was trained by her father, Orazio — a painter who had absorbed the dramatic lighting of Caravaggio. Women were barred from the academies where artists studied anatomy and drew from the nude model, and most female painters of the period confined themselves to portraits and still lifes. Ⓐ<u>She</u> chose instead the large, crowded scenes from history and scripture that were regarded as the most prestigious genre, and she executed them with a vehemence that astonished her contemporaries.
Her early life was marked by a notorious trial. In 1612 her father brought a case against the painter Agostino Tassi, his collaborator and her tutor in perspective, for raping her. During the proceedings, which lasted months, Ⓑ<u>she</u> was questioned under thumbscrews — a common method of testing a witness's veracity. Tassi was convicted, though his sentence was never enforced. Soon afterward she married and moved to Florence, where in 1616 she became the first woman admitted to the city's Academy of the Arts of Drawing (Accademia delle Arti del Disegno).
For centuries she was remembered, if at all, chiefly as Orazio's daughter, and several of Ⓒ<u>his</u> paintings were attributed to her and vice versa. Her rediscovery began in the twentieth century, and feminist art historians of the 1970s brought her work renewed attention. Her depictions of Judith beheading the Assyrian general Holofernes, in which the heroine and her maid grip the struggling man with startling physical resolve, became her most celebrated works, and many critics have read them as a response to her own ordeal.
Recent scholars, however, caution against reducing her art to biography. Artemisia was a shrewd professional who negotiated with powerful patrons across Italy and even in London, where Ⓓ<u>she</u> joined her father at the court of Charles I in the late 1630s. Her letters reveal an artist acutely conscious of her worth, who insisted that her work be judged by the same standards as that of men.

For much of human history, goiter — a swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck — was so prevalent in certain regions that it was regarded almost as a normal feature of local appearance. In parts of the Alps, the Himalayas, and the Great Lakes region of North America, a large share of the population was afflicted. The cause, established gradually during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, was a deficiency of iodine, an element the thyroid needs to manufacture hormones that regulate metabolism and the development of the brain. Iodine is plentiful in seawater, but in areas once scoured by glaciers or repeatedly flooded, it has been leached from the soil, and crops grown there contain little of it.
The consequences extended far beyond the visible swelling. Severe deficiency during pregnancy could cause profound intellectual disability and stunted growth in the child, and even mild deficiency in childhood is associated with diminished cognitive performance. Because the damage accrued silently, communities often failed to recognize how much potential was being squandered.
The remedy turned out to be remarkably cheap. Swiss authorities began adding iodine to table salt in the 1920s, and in 1924 iodized salt went on sale in Michigan, one of the American states where goiter was endemic. Within a few years the prevalence of goiter in affected areas fell dramatically. Salt was an ideal vehicle — nearly everyone consumes it (in fairly consistent amounts), and adding iodine costs a pittance per person each year.
In the following decades, international agencies promoted universal salt iodization, and today the great majority of households worldwide use iodized salt. Some economists have hailed it as one of the most cost-effective public health measures ever devised, and studies of the American program have linked it to measurable gains in the cognitive outcomes of children born in previously deficient areas. Its success carries a lesson for policy — an intervention need not be dramatic to be transformative, provided it is ____ enough to reach almost everyone.

Imagine a heap of sand containing a million grains. Remove a single grain, and you still have a heap; one grain, surely, cannot make the difference between a heap and a non-heap. Remove another, and the same reasoning applies. Yet if you continue long enough, you will be left with a solitary grain, which is plainly not a heap. Somewhere a heap must have ceased to exist, but there seems to be no grain whose removal was responsible. This puzzle (attributed to the ancient Greek philosopher Eubulides of Miletus) is known as the sorites paradox, from the Greek word for heap.
The paradox arises because many of our concepts are vague. Words such as tall, bald, rich, and old apply clearly to some cases and clearly fail to apply to others, but they also have <u>borderline</u> cases in which no answer seems correct. A man with a hundred thousand hairs is not bald and a man with none is, but how many hairs mark the boundary? Insisting on a precise number seems arbitrary, yet denying that there is any boundary seems to lead straight to absurdity.
Philosophers have proposed several responses. Epistemicists maintain that there is in fact a sharp boundary — a precise number of grains at which a heap ceases to be one — but that we are incapable of knowing where it lies. Others propose degrees of truth, so that the statement that something is a heap becomes gradually less true as grains are removed. Still others hold that vague statements are neither true nor false in borderline cases. Each solution exacts a cost, and none commands general assent.
The puzzle has practical ramifications. Laws must often draw sharp lines through vague territory, stipulating, for example, the precise age at which a person may vote or the exact speed at which driving becomes illegal. Such lines are admittedly arbitrary, but a society that refused to draw them would find itself paralyzed. The paradox thus reminds us that precision is sometimes a convenience we impose on a world that does not supply it.

Most of the world's writing systems evolved gradually over centuries, shaped by countless anonymous scribes. The Korean alphabet is a striking exception. It was devised under the direction of King Sejong and promulgated in 1446 in a document titled Hunminjeongeum, meaning the correct sounds for the instruction of the people. Before then, Koreans wrote with Chinese characters, a system ill suited to the Korean language and so demanding that literacy was largely confined to a small, educated elite.
The new script was remarkable for its design. Its basic consonant letters were modeled on the shape of the speech organs used to pronounce them — the letter for the k sound depicts the root of the tongue blocking the throat, and the letter for n depicts the tip of the tongue touching the ridge behind the upper teeth. Further consonants were derived by adding strokes to these basic shapes, so that related sounds look related on the page. Vowels were built from three elements representing heaven, earth, and humanity. Letters are grouped into syllable blocks, preserving the visual rhythm of Chinese writing while recording sounds rather than meanings.
The innovation encountered resistance. Some scholar-officials objected that abandoning Chinese characters would estrange Korea from the civilization of China and debase learning. For centuries the script was used chiefly by women, commoners, and authors of popular literature, while official documents and serious scholarship continued in classical Chinese. Only in the late nineteenth century, amid rising national consciousness, did it acquire official status, and it became the predominant script of Korean public life in the twentieth century.
Linguists have frequently praised the alphabet as one of the most ingeniously engineered writing systems ever devised, and its creation is commemorated in South Korea by a national holiday on October 9. Its history also illustrates a broader point — a writing system is not merely a technical tool but a social institution, and its fate depends as much on politics and prestige as on design.

English speakers who say they, them, and their every few seconds rarely pause to consider that these humble pronouns are not native to their language. They were borrowed from Old Norse, the tongue of the Scandinavian settlers who began raiding the coasts of Britain in the late eighth century. These settlers later occupied a broad swath of northern and eastern England — a region known as the Danelaw. Borrowing pronouns is exceedingly rare. Languages typically import words for novel objects or institutions, not the basic grammatical machinery of everyday speech. That English did so testifies to an unusually <u>intimate</u> coexistence between two peoples.
Old English and Old Norse were closely related Germanic languages, and their speakers could probably understand each other in a rudimentary way. In mixed communities, where Anglo-Saxon and Scandinavian families intermarried and traded, speakers seem to have simplified their speech to make it mutually intelligible. Some scholars argue that this contact accelerated the erosion of the elaborate inflectional endings that distinguished Old English from the far simpler grammar of modern English, though the extent of Norse responsibility remains disputed.
The vocabulary bequeathed by the settlers is strikingly ordinary. Sky, egg, knife, window, skin, and husband all derive from Norse (as do the verbs take, get, and call). In some cases a Norse word ousted its English counterpart; in others both survived with diverging meanings, so that English now possesses shirt and skirt, originally the same word in its Old English and Norse guises. Place names tell a similar story — hundreds of towns in northern England end in -by, the Norse word for a farmstead or village, as in Derby and Whitby.
The Normans who conquered England in 1066 contributed a larger and more prestigious vocabulary of law, cuisine, and government. Yet it is the Scandinavians, whose legacy is woven into the most commonplace words, who arguably left the deeper imprint on the structure of the language.

Every year the world discards a staggering quantity of electrical and electronic equipment — smartphones replaced after two or three years, laptops that no longer receive software updates, refrigerators, toasters, cables, toys with flashing lights, and disposable vapes thrown away after a few days of use. According to the Global E-waste Monitor published by United Nations agencies in 2024, humanity generated about sixty-two million tonnes of such waste in 2022 (an increase of more than eighty percent since 2010). The report projected that the figure could reach eighty-two million tonnes by 2030.
Only a fraction of this refuse is handled responsibly. The same report found that less than a quarter of the e-waste generated in 2022 was documented as properly collected and recycled. The remainder was hoarded in drawers and attics, buried in landfills, incinerated, or shipped, sometimes illicitly, to countries where informal workers dismantle devices by hand. In such settings, cables are often burned in the open air to recover copper, releasing toxic fumes, and circuit boards are soaked in acid baths, exposing workers, many of them children, to lead, mercury, and other hazardous substances.
The waste also represents economic profligacy on a grand scale. Discarded electronics contain gold, silver, copper, and scarce metals indispensable to the energy transition. The report valued the metals in the 2022 e-waste at tens of billions of dollars. Recovering them, however, is technically ____: devices are designed to be compact and sealed rather than readily disassembled, and the precious materials are present in minute quantities dispersed across dozens of components.
Policymakers have begun to respond. The European Union now mandates a common charging port for many portable devices, a measure intended to reduce the number of superfluous chargers that end up in drawers and bins, and several jurisdictions oblige manufacturers to make spare parts and repair manuals available. Advocates contend that the most effective remedy lies upstream, in products engineered to last longer and to be mended rather than replaced.

The fountain pen arrived in a shoebox wrapped in brown paper, three weeks after my grandfather's funeral, with no letter enclosed, only a card bearing my name in his angular, slanting hand. It was black, scratched along the barrel, and so heavy that I first mistook it for a tool. My mother said he had bought it in 1962, the year he passed the examination that allowed him to leave the village and train as a schoolteacher, and that he had used it every day for half a century.
I had no idea what to make of it. I typed my essays, sent messages with my thumbs, and could not remember the last time I had written more than a shopping list by hand. The first time I filled it, ink flooded my fingers and blotted the page. The nib, worn to the angle of his grip after fifty years, felt <u>recalcitrant</u> in mine; my letters lurched and skidded across the paper as if the pen were resisting a stranger.
Yet I persisted, perhaps out of guilt. Every evening I copied a few paragraphs from whatever book I was reading, slowly, because the pen punished haste. After a month the ink stopped pooling. After two, I noticed that I had begun to compose sentences in my head before committing them to paper, weighing words with a deliberation I had never practiced at a keyboard, where every error could be deleted without a trace.
I still use the pen, though not for everything. It has never become entirely mine; the nib still tugs slightly toward an angle that is not quite my own. I have come to think of that small resistance as a kind of conversation, the only one with him that I am still able to have.

In 1984 the biologist Katy Payne was observing elephants at a zoo in Portland, Oregon, when she noticed a faint throbbing in the air — a sensation she compared to the deepest notes of a pipe organ. She suspected that the animals were producing sounds too low for human ears to detect. Recordings made with specialized equipment confirmed her hunch — elephants communicate extensively through infrasound, vibrations below about twenty hertz (the lower threshold of human hearing).
Low-frequency sound has a remarkable property. Because its long waves are absorbed and scattered far less than high-pitched sounds by vegetation and terrain, it can travel great distances. Researchers in Africa have estimated that under favorable conditions, particularly in the cool, still air of evening, elephant rumbles may be audible to other elephants several kilometers away. This capacity helps explain observations that had long puzzled field biologists — scattered family groups that seemed to coordinate their movements without any visible signal, and males that appeared to converge on receptive females from far beyond the range of sight or smell.
Subsequent research has revealed that elephants may also ____ these vibrations through the ground. Rumbles propagate through the soil as seismic waves, and elephants have been observed freezing in place, leaning forward, and pressing their trunks to the earth or lifting a foot when such signals arrive, as if listening with their entire bodies. Sensitive receptors in the feet and trunk are thought to register the vibrations, and the dense bones of the skull may conduct them to the inner ear. I once stood beside an enclosure while a keeper played back one of these recordings, and I felt it in my chest before I could say whether I had heard anything.
The discoveries have practical ramifications. Conservationists now deploy acoustic monitors in forests where elephants are difficult to observe directly, estimating their numbers and tracking their movements by their calls. Because the same devices also record gunshots, researchers have explored whether they can help rangers locate poachers before more animals are slaughtered.

In 1720 Britain experienced one of the most spectacular financial manias in its history. The South Sea Company (founded in 1711) had been granted a monopoly on British trade with Spanish America, a privilege of little real value given that Britain and Spain were frequently at war and Spain jealously restricted foreign commerce. The company's true business was finance. In 1720 it persuaded Parliament to approve a scheme under which it would assume a large part of the national debt, offering holders of government bonds the chance to exchange them for South Sea shares.
The scheme depended on a rising share price, and the directors did everything in their power to ensure one. They circulated rumors of fabulous profits from trade, lent money to investors so that they could buy still more shares, and offered shares to politicians on favorable terms to secure their support. The price climbed from about one hundred and thirty pounds early in the year to roughly one thousand pounds by the summer. The frenzy spilled over into dozens of other ventures, some of them patently dubious, prompting Parliament to pass an act requiring new joint-stock companies to obtain a royal charter, a measure the South Sea Company itself had supported in order to (A) ____ competition for investors' money.
When confidence faltered in the late summer, the price collapsed, falling below two hundred pounds by the end of the year. Thousands of investors were ruined. A parliamentary inquiry uncovered bribery and fraud, several directors had their estates confiscated, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer was expelled from the House of Commons and imprisoned. Robert Walpole, who managed the aftermath and restored a measure of stability, rose to become the dominant political figure of the following two decades.
Historians continue to debate how irrational the episode was. Some emphasize mass delusion; others note that many investors bought shares expecting to sell them to others at even higher prices, a strategy that is perfectly rational for each individual so long as the price keeps rising but (B) ____ for the market as a whole.

Imagine that a stranger is handed a hundred dollars and told to offer you some portion of it. If you accept the offer, the money is divided as proposed; if you reject it, neither of you receives anything. Standard economic theory, which assumes that people seek to maximize their own gain, makes a stark prediction — the proposer should offer the smallest possible amount, and you should accept it, since a single dollar is better than nothing. This scenario — known as the ultimatum game — was first studied experimentally by German economists in 1982, and the results flatly contradicted the theory.
In experiments conducted mainly with university students in industrialized countries, proposers typically offered between forty and fifty percent of the sum, and responders frequently rejected offers below about twenty percent, forfeiting real money in order to punish what they perceived as unfairness. The pattern proved remarkably robust, persisting even when the stakes were raised substantially. Many researchers concluded that a sense of fairness, and a willingness to pay a price to enforce it, is a deep-seated feature of human psychology.
A team of anthropologists and economists then put that conclusion to a more demanding test by taking the game to fifteen small-scale societies around the world. The results (published in 2001) were strikingly <u>heterogeneous</u>. Among the Machiguenga (horticulturalists of the Peruvian Amazon who rarely cooperate beyond the family), offers averaged about a quarter of the stake and were almost never rejected. Among the whale hunters of Lamalera in Indonesia, whose livelihood depends on large cooperative crews, average offers exceeded half. In two groups in Papua New Guinea, where accepting a gift can create an onerous obligation to reciprocate, some generous offers were actually refused.
The researchers found that offers tended to be higher in societies more integrated into markets and more dependent on cooperation with non-kin. Fairness, it seems, is not a fixed quantity but a norm calibrated by the economic and social life of a community. The findings also served as a caution against treating students in a handful of wealthy countries as representative of humanity at large.

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed a stark imbalance in the global production of vaccines. By the end of 2021, wealthy countries had vaccinated a large majority of their adult populations, while in many low-income countries only a small percentage of people had received even a single dose. COVAX — an international initiative created to ensure equitable access — delivered well over a billion doses before it was wound down at the end of 2023. It repeatedly found itself at the back of the queue, however, as rich governments that had signed advance contracts with manufacturers received their supplies first.
For Africa the episode underscored a longstanding vulnerability. The continent produces only a tiny fraction of the vaccines it uses (roughly one percent by commonly cited estimates) and depends overwhelmingly on imports. When export restrictions and soaring demand constricted supply in 2021, African health systems had little recourse. The African Union subsequently set a goal of manufacturing sixty percent of the continent's vaccines locally by 2040, and in 2024 the vaccine alliance Gavi launched the African Vaccine Manufacturing Accelerator — a financing mechanism offering up to 1.2 billion dollars over ten years to support fledgling producers.
Building a vaccine industry from scratch is a formidable undertaking. Plants are costly, regulatory agencies must be strengthened to approve their products, and manufacturers need reliable buyers to remain viable between emergencies, when demand evaporates. A World Health Organization project established in South Africa in 2021 sought to share messenger RNA technology with manufacturers in lower-income countries, enabling them to develop their own products rather than waiting for licenses.
Governments have also attempted to codify lessons at the international level. In May 2025 the World Health Assembly adopted a Pandemic Agreement intended to improve prevention, preparedness, and the equitable distribution of medical products in future emergencies, though several crucial details — including rules for sharing pathogens and the benefits derived from them — were deferred to further negotiation. Whether these commitments will withstand the pressures of the next crisis remains to be seen.

The sonnet — a poem of fourteen lines — was perfected in thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Italy, and its most influential practitioner was Francesco Petrarch, Ⓐ<u>whose</u> poems to an idealized beloved named Laura set the pattern for European love poetry for two centuries. The Petrarchan sonnet divides into an octave of eight lines and a sestet of six. The octave typically poses a problem or describes a predicament, and at the ninth line comes a turn, the volta, in which the poem changes direction, Ⓑ<u>offering</u> a resolution, a reversal, or a deepening of the opening thought.
The form arrived in England in the early sixteenth century through the translations of Sir Thomas Wyatt — a diplomat who encountered Petrarch's work during missions to Italy. English, however, is comparatively poor in rhyming words, and the Italian rhyme scheme (which requires the octave to repeat only two rhymes) proved <u>onerous</u> to sustain. Wyatt's younger contemporary Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, devised an alternative Ⓒ<u>that</u> was better suited to the language — three quatrains of four lines, each with its own pair of rhymes, followed by a concluding couplet.
This English form is now associated above all with Shakespeare, whose 154 sonnets, Ⓓ<u>publishing</u> in 1609, exploit its structure brilliantly. The final couplet can deliver an epigrammatic summary, a witty twist, or an ironic undercutting of everything that precedes it. Some critics complain that the couplet encourages glib conclusions; others admire the tension between the meditative quatrains and the abrupt finality of the last two lines. Like many students, I first met the form as a set of rules to be memorized.
Over the following centuries poets continually reinvented the form. Milton turned it toward politics and religion, the Romantics revived it after a period of neglect, and modern writers have stretched it almost beyond recognition, discarding rhyme or meter while retaining the compressed argument of fourteen lines. Its longevity suggests that constraint, far from stifling invention, can provoke it.

In the early nineteenth century, transporting living plants across oceans was a frustrating enterprise. Seedlings carried on the decks of sailing ships were battered by salt spray, scorched by tropical sun, and starved of fresh water, and most perished long before they reached their destination. [A] Botanists lamented that only a tiny fraction of the specimens dispatched from distant colonies survived the journey.
The solution was discovered by accident. Around 1829 Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward — a London physician with a passion for natural history — buried the chrysalis of a moth in moist soil inside a sealed glass bottle. Some weeks later he noticed that a fern and a grass had sprouted in the soil and were flourishing, although he had never watered them. Inside the closed container, moisture evaporated from the soil and leaves, condensed on the glass, and trickled back down, creating a self-sustaining miniature climate. [B]
Ward commissioned larger glazed cases and, in 1833, sent two of them filled with plants on a voyage to Australia. They arrived months later in excellent condition, and the cases, restocked with Australian plants, made the return voyage just as successfully. [C] The Wardian case (as it came to be called) soon became standard equipment for botanical gardens and commercial nurseries, and a fashionable ornament in Victorian parlors.
Its consequences were far-reaching. In 1848 the Scottish botanist Robert Fortune was employed by the East India Company to obtain tea plants and seeds from China, where their export was jealously guarded, and he shipped thousands of them to India in Wardian cases, helping to establish the tea industry of the Himalayan foothills. [D] Historians have therefore described the humble glass box as an instrument of empire, one that enabled colonial powers to ____ lucrative crops from their native regions to territories under their own control, often to the detriment of the countries from which they were taken.

Basketball players and fans have long believed in the hot hand — the notion that a player who has made several shots in a row is more likely than usual to make the next one. In 1985 the psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone, and Amos Tversky set out to test this belief. Analyzing shooting records from a professional team and conducting controlled experiments with college players, they found no evidence that success followed success more often than chance would predict. Streaks occurred, but no more frequently than they would in a random sequence of hits and misses — much as a fair coin occasionally produces several heads in a row.
The study became a celebrated example of a cognitive illusion. People, the authors argued, expect random sequences to alternate more than they actually do, and so they perceive meaningful patterns in streaks that are merely the product of chance. Coaches and players remained unconvinced, but among psychologists and economists the hot hand fallacy became a textbook illustration of human irrationality.
Three decades later the conclusion was challenged from an unexpected quarter. In a paper first circulated in 2015, the economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo demonstrated that the method used in the original analysis contained a subtle statistical bias. When one examines a finite sequence of coin flips and calculates the proportion of heads that immediately follow a run of heads, the expected result is actually below fifty percent rather than equal to it. A player whose accuracy after streaks merely matched his overall average was therefore performing better than a truly random shooter would. Correcting for the bias, Miller and Sanjurjo found evidence of a modest hot hand in the original experimental data.
The reversal has been widely discussed as a lesson in humility. Researchers who had exposed a supposed flaw in ordinary intuition had themselves relied on an intuition about probability that proved mistaken. Whether the hot hand in real games is large enough to matter remains contested, but the episode suggests that claims of irrationality deserve as much scrutiny as the beliefs they disparage.

At 8:01 on the morning of June 26, 1974, a cashier at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, passed a ten-pack of chewing gum over a scanner, and a computer registered its price. The purchase (it cost sixty-seven cents) is commonly cited as the first commercial scan of a product bearing a Universal Product Code, the pattern of black bars and white spaces that now adorns almost every packaged item on earth.
The notion of encoding information in printed lines had been patented more than two decades earlier, but it languished for want of affordable technology to read the codes. Two developments made it practicable — inexpensive lasers and increasingly powerful computers. Equally important was an agreement among American grocery manufacturers and retailers, reached in 1973 after protracted negotiations, to adopt a single standard. Without such consensus, a code printed by a cereal company would be useless to a store whose scanner could not interpret it.
Adoption was initially <u>sluggish</u>. Stores were reluctant to invest in costly scanners before many products carried codes, while manufacturers hesitated to print codes until enough stores could read them — a classic chicken-and-egg dilemma. Some consumers also distrusted the change, fearing that the removal of price stickers from individual items would make it easier for stores to overcharge. I still remember my mother peeling price stickers off jars at the kitchen table. By the early 1980s, however, the benefits had become ____: checkout lines moved faster, errors declined, and retailers gained an unprecedented, item-by-item record of what sold, when, and where.
That last advantage proved the most consequential. Detailed sales data allowed retailers to manage inventory with precision, to negotiate with suppliers from a position of strength, and to identify which products deserved prime shelf space. Some historians argue that the barcode helped shift power in the consumer economy from manufacturers to large retail chains — a shift whose effects are still palpable. The modest pack of gum that inaugurated this transformation now resides in a museum collection in Washington.

Between 1980 and 1994, conservators working for the Vatican cleaned the frescoes that Michelangelo painted on the ceiling and altar wall of the Sistine Chapel. The artist had completed the ceiling in 1512, and Ⓐ<u>he</u> returned more than two decades later to paint the Last Judgment on the wall behind the altar. Over the centuries the paintings had been dimmed by candle smoke, dust, and layers of animal glue and varnish applied by earlier restorers Ⓑ<u>who</u> had hoped to brighten them. As the grime was removed, colors emerged that startled many viewers — vivid pinks, acid greens, and luminous oranges where generations of scholars had admired somber, sculptural browns.
The project provoked a bitter controversy. A number of artists and critics argued that the restorers were removing not only dirt but also a final layer of shading that Michelangelo Ⓒ<u>himself</u> had added in glue-based paint after the plaster dried — a technique known as a secco. Without it, they contended, the figures had lost their depth and modeling, and the ceiling had been reduced to a garish cartoon. Some petitioned the Vatican to halt the work.
The restorers and their supporters rejected these charges. They maintained that close examination revealed no systematic retouching of that kind on the ceiling, and that the dark layers removed were the residue of later interventions and centuries of pollution. The brilliant palette, they argued, was consistent with the practice of Florentine painters of the period and with Ⓓ<u>his</u> own training. Photographs were taken at every stage so that the work could be scrutinized by others.
The dispute has never been entirely resolved, partly because what was removed cannot be examined again. Yet it altered the way many scholars understand the artist. Michelangelo had long been regarded as a sculptor who painted almost reluctantly, favoring form over color; the cleaned frescoes suggested a bold colorist as well. The debate also prompted conservators elsewhere to document their methods more meticulously — an outcome that both camps could applaud.

In 1806 a young Boston merchant named Frederic Tudor dispatched a ship loaded with ice cut from a New England pond to the Caribbean island of Martinique. Acquaintances regarded the venture as preposterous, and their skepticism seemed vindicated — much of the cargo melted, local buyers had no means of storing what remained, and Tudor lost a considerable sum. Over the following years his debts mounted so precipitously that he was more than once confined in a debtors' prison.
Tudor persisted, and he gradually solved the problems that had doomed his first voyage. He built insulated icehouses at his destinations so that ice could be stored and sold over weeks rather than hours. He discovered that sawdust — a worthless by-product of New England's lumber mills — made an excellent and cheap insulator for cargo in ships' holds. Collaborators developed a horse-drawn cutter that scored the frozen surface of a pond into uniform blocks, which packed tightly and melted more slowly than irregular chunks. Equally important, Tudor cultivated demand, offering free cold drinks to bartenders and teaching customers in hot climates to regard chilled beverages as a necessity rather than a luxury.
By the 1830s the trade had become lucrative. In 1833 a ship carrying ice from Massachusetts reached Calcutta after a voyage of some four months, with a substantial part of its cargo intact, and ice from New England was soon sold in ports across the tropics. By mid-century the harvesting of natural ice employed thousands of workers, and Tudor (once derided) was celebrated as the Ice King.
The business did not endure. In the late nineteenth century mechanical refrigeration matured, and manufactured ice, which could be produced anywhere and was free of the contamination that increasingly afflicted ponds near growing cities, steadily displaced the harvested kind. Yet the ice trade left a lasting legacy — it habituated consumers to cold food and drink and created the expectation on which the refrigeration industry would later build.

Few moral philosophies have been stated more crisply than utilitarianism. Its founder, the English reformer Jeremy Bentham, proposed in 1789 that the rightness of an action, or of a law, should be judged solely by its consequences for human happiness, understood as the balance of pleasure over pain. He even sketched a felicific calculus for measuring pleasures according to their intensity, duration, certainty, and other dimensions. Pushpin — a simple children's game — was in his view as valuable as poetry if it yielded as much pleasure.
Bentham's doctrine had a radical edge. Because every person's happiness counted equally, it furnished an argument against laws that served the privileged few at the expense of the many. Bentham applied it to prisons, the treatment of animals, and the reform of Parliament. Detractors, however, derided it as a philosophy fit for swine, since it seemed to place the crudest physical gratifications on a level with the noblest pursuits of the mind.
John Stuart Mill (who had been raised by his father as a disciple of Bentham) attempted to rebut this charge in his essay Utilitarianism, first published in 1861. Pleasures, he argued, differ in quality as well as quantity; anyone acquainted with both intellectual and sensual pleasures will prefer the former, even at the cost of some discontent. Hence his famous declaration that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.
Mill's <u>amendment</u> has been admired and criticized in equal measure. Admirers regard it as a humane refinement that rescues utilitarianism from vulgarity. Critics object that once qualities of pleasure are introduced, the theory no longer rests on a single measurable standard, since judging that one pleasure is higher than another appears to require some value other than pleasure itself. The debate continues to reverberate in contemporary ethics, from cost-benefit analysis in public policy to arguments about effective charitable giving.

In 1961 Jane Jacobs — a journalist without formal training in planning — published The Death and Life of Great American Cities, a book that challenged the reigning orthodoxy of urban renewal. At the time, planners in the United States were demolishing entire neighborhoods they regarded as slums and replacing them with expressways and towers set in open lawns. Their premise was that light, air, and the segregation of functions would cure social ills. Jacobs, who lived in the dense, mixed neighborhood of Greenwich Village in New York, argued that these planners had fundamentally misunderstood what makes cities work.
Her central insight concerned safety. Streets are safe, she contended, not because of police patrols or empty spaces but because of what she called eyes on the street — the continuous, informal surveillance provided by shopkeepers, residents looking out of windows, and passersby. Such vigilance requires a mixture of uses (shops, homes, bars, and workplaces) so that people are present at all hours. The sterile plazas of the housing projects, deserted for much of the day, offered no such protection and often became more perilous than the crowded blocks they replaced. Walking through such a neighborhood today, I find her argument almost self-evident.
Jacobs also extolled short blocks, buildings of varied age, and a density that planners deplored as congestion. Old buildings, she observed, provided cheap space for fledgling businesses that could not afford new construction. Diversity, in her account, was not a nuisance to be eradicated but the very engine of urban vitality.
Her ideas were initially dismissed by many professionals, but she proved a formidable activist, helping to defeat a plan to drive an expressway through lower Manhattan. Today her principles are so widely accepted that critics worry about an ironic consequence — the lively, walkable neighborhoods she championed have become so coveted that soaring rents are displacing the very residents and small businesses that made them vibrant.

For most of history, aging was deemed an inexorable fact of life rather than a process that medicine might alter. That assumption is now being challenged by a burgeoning field known as geroscience (the study of how aging drives disease). Its central proposition is that many of the ailments that afflict the elderly, including heart disease, dementia, and several cancers, share common biological roots in the insidious deterioration of cells and tissues, and that slowing this deterioration might postpone all of them at once.
Laboratory findings have kindled considerable optimism. Researchers have extended the lifespans of worms, flies, and mice by altering single genes, by restricting their calories, and by administering drugs such as rapamycin. Other experiments have targeted senescent cells — damaged cells that stop dividing but linger in tissues, secreting substances that promote inflammation; eliminating them has improved several measures of health in elderly mice. Investors have been quick to take notice. In recent years wealthy technology entrepreneurs have poured billions of dollars into companies devoted to understanding and reversing aging, and one such firm was launched in 2022 with three billion dollars in funding.
Skeptics counsel caution. Results in short-lived laboratory animals seldom translate neatly to human beings, and trials that measured lifespan directly in people would be prohibitively protracted. Some researchers have therefore espoused a more modest goal — extending healthspan, the years lived in good health, rather than lifespan itself. A proposed trial of metformin — an inexpensive diabetes drug — was designed in part to persuade regulators that aging, or at least a cluster of age-related diseases, could serve as a legitimate target for treatment.
Critics also voice ethical qualms. If costly therapies became available, they might widen already <u>conspicuous</u> gaps in life expectancy between rich and poor, and populations that lived much longer would impose fresh burdens on pensions and health systems. Proponents retort that even partial success could alleviate immense suffering, since a treatment that delayed the onset of several diseases at once would benefit far more people than a cure for any single one.

English is unusually replete with pairs of words that descend from the same ancestor but entered the language by different routes. Linguists call them doublets. Frail and fragile both come from the Latin fragilis; the first arrived through Old French in the Middle Ages, abraded by centuries of colloquial speech, while the second was borrowed directly from Latin by later scholars, preserving a form much closer to the original. Royal and regal, loyal and legal, and sure and secure (all from Latin) form similar pairs. In each case the word that passed through French is shorter and more eroded, whereas the learned borrowing retains more of its Latin shape.
Doublets also arise when the same word is borrowed more than once. Chief and chef both derive from the Latin word for head — the first entered English from Old French in the Middle Ages, the second from modern French in the nineteenth century, when English diners adopted French culinary vocabulary. Guard and ward share a Germanic origin; ward is native English, while guard reached English through French, whose speakers turned the initial w sound into gu. A similar difference between Norman and central French dialects produced warranty and guarantee.
What makes doublets linguistically intriguing is that the members of a pair seldom remain synonyms. Languages tend to resist exact redundancy, and speakers gradually assign a different meaning or register to each form. Frail usually describes the body, fragile objects and situations. Regal connotes grandeur, royal mere membership in a royal family. Hospital and hostel (both derived from a Latin word related to hospes, 'guest') now denote entirely different institutions, and hotel, borrowed later from modern French, adds a third.
For historians of the language, doublets function as a kind of stratigraphy. Just as layers of rock record successive geological epochs, parallel forms reveal successive waves of contact and borrowing. A single Latin root, encountered at disparate moments, can leave several discrete deposits in the vocabulary.

Dear Seo-yeon,
Your mother tells me you have chosen your dormitory and bought a desk lamp that folds flat, and that you are nervous. Good. Nervousness means you understand that something important is about to happen. I was nervous every morning for the first year I ran the shop, and I ran it for thirty-eight.
You will not remember the shop well; you were six when I closed it. It was a narrow room above a pharmacy, with two sewing machines, a long cutting table, and a mirror that made everyone look slightly taller (which I never repaired, for obvious commercial reasons). People brought me suits to alter for weddings and funerals, school uniforms to lengthen every spring, coats they could not afford to replace. I learned more about the town from hems and seams than any newspaper could have divulged. A jacket let out twice in one year meant prosperity or poor health; a dress taken in meant grief, or love.
What I want to tell you is this. The most valuable thing I possessed was not my skill, which was ordinary, but my habit of measuring twice. Young tailors always want to cut. The cloth is right there, the scissors are sharp, the customer is waiting. But a cut cannot be undone, and an hour of forbearance at the table spares a week of remorse. You are about to be surrounded by clever people who will urge you to decide quickly what you believe and who you are. Measure twice. Ask the question again. There is no shame in being slow if what you make fits.
I have enclosed a small pair of scissors. They were my first. They will not help you with chemistry, but they will remind you of an old woman who is very proud of you.
With love,
Grandmother

The blueness of the sky seems too obvious to require explanation, yet the question preoccupied some of the finest scientific minds of the nineteenth century. Sunlight appears white because it contains a mixture of all the colors of the visible spectrum, from long-wavelength red to short-wavelength violet. As this light passes through the atmosphere, it encounters molecules of nitrogen and oxygen vastly smaller than the wavelengths of light themselves. In 1871 the British physicist John William Strutt (Lord Rayleigh) showed mathematically that such minute particles scatter light with an intensity that rises steeply as wavelength decreases (in proportion to the inverse fourth power of the wavelength). Blue light, with its shorter wavelength, is therefore scattered several times more strongly than red, and it reaches our eyes from every direction of the sky.
An obvious objection ensues. If shorter wavelengths scatter more, the sky ought to look violet rather than blue. Several factors explain why it does not. Sunlight contains less violet than blue to begin with, a little violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and the human eye is considerably less sensitive to violet than to blue. The perceived color is thus a joint product of physics and physiology.
The same principle accounts for the reds and oranges of sunrise and sunset. When the sun is low, its light must traverse a far longer path through the atmosphere before reaching an observer. Along the way, most of the blue is scattered out of the direct beam, leaving the longer wavelengths to ____. Dust, smoke, and volcanic ash can accentuate the effect, which is why sunsets following major eruptions are often unusually lurid.
Clouds, by contrast, are white because their water droplets are much larger than the wavelengths of visible light. Such droplets scatter all colors more or less indiscriminately — a regime described by a different theory — so the light they send toward us retains the mixture of the original sunlight. On the Moon, which has no atmosphere to scatter sunlight, the daytime sky is black.

Cities have always been prone to inundation, but the peril is mutating in character. As the climate warms, the atmosphere can hold more moisture (roughly seven percent more for each degree Celsius of warming), and intense downpours are becoming more frequent in many regions. At the same time, the spread of pavement and buildings has sealed the ground that once absorbed rainfall, so that water races across streets toward drainage systems designed for the climate of decades past.
Underground spaces have proved especially perilous. In August 2022 record rainfall in Seoul flooded semi-basement apartments (known in Korean as banjiha) and several residents who could not escape drowned in their homes. The tragedy prompted the city government to announce that it would phase out such dwellings as residences. Comparable disasters have struck elsewhere — in September 2021 the remnants of Hurricane Ida killed eleven people in basement apartments in New York City, and in October 2024 flash floods around Valencia, in eastern Spain, killed more than two hundred people, some of whom were trapped in underground garages after going to move their cars.
The danger in such spaces <u>escalates</u> with startling speed. Water inundating a basement can rise to the ceiling within minutes, and the pressure of water against a door can render it impossible to open from within. Electricity may fail, and occupants may remain oblivious to the threat until escape is foreclosed. Subway systems face analogous risks, and several cities have installed floodgates at station entrances.
Engineers increasingly contend that the remedy cannot rely on ever larger pipes alone. Instead, many cities are pursuing what is sometimes called the sponge approach — rehabilitating wetlands, building parks and plazas designed to flood harmlessly, installing permeable pavement, and constructing underground reservoirs that store stormwater temporarily. The vast drainage tunnels and holding tanks of the Tokyo area (completed in 2006) are often invoked as a paradigm. Yet the poorest residents, who are most likely to live in basements and low-lying districts, are often the last to benefit from such investments, a pattern that transmutes a natural hazard into a question of social justice.

Long before email, the great cities of the nineteenth century experimented with a strikingly physical way of sending messages quickly — blowing them through tubes. In 1853 a telegraph company in London installed a short pneumatic line to carry written telegrams between its central office and the stock exchange, sparing the couriers who had previously scurried through the congested streets. The principle was rudimentary. A message was rolled into a cylindrical container and inserted into a tube, and air pressure or a vacuum propelled it to its destination at speeds that could exceed those of any horse-drawn carriage.
Paris developed the most extensive and enduring system. Beginning in 1866, engineers laid tubes beneath the city's streets (often through the sewers), and by the early twentieth century the network extended for hundreds of kilometers, linking post offices throughout the capital. Parisians could send a pneumatique, a small card or letter that would typically arrive across the city within a couple of hours. The service became interwoven with the city's social fabric, carrying business messages, invitations, and declarations of love, and it appears in the novels and films of the period as an emblem of urgency.
The networks were exorbitantly expensive to maintain, however. Tubes ruptured, canisters jammed, and the pumps devoured prodigious amounts of energy. As the telephone spread through middle-class homes in the twentieth century, demand gradually waned, and fax machines later offered a faster alternative for documents. Paris finally <u>discontinued</u> its pneumatic post in 1984, after more than a century of service. Similar systems in Berlin, Vienna, and Prague met the same fate, although part of the Prague network survived until it was damaged by flooding in 2002.
Pneumatic tubes have not become entirely obsolete. Many hospitals use them to dispatch blood samples and medications between departments, and some banks still rely on them at drive-through windows. Historians of technology note that the tubes presaged a distinctly modern preoccupation — the desire to move information across a city faster than people themselves can travel.

Many of the most illustrious novels of Victorian England were not first published as books at all. Charles Dickens's career was launched in 1836 with The Pickwick Papers, which appeared in monthly installments of thirty-two pages (each costing a shilling and bound in green paper covers). Sales of the early numbers were lackluster, but after Dickens introduced the comic servant Sam Weller in the fourth installment, demand soared, and by the end of the run the publisher was printing some forty thousand copies of each part. Serial publication would remain the backbone of Dickens's career, and contemporaries such as William Makepeace Thackeray and Elizabeth Gaskell published in much the same way.
The format conferred economic advantages. Readers who could not afford a complete novel in three volumes (which typically cost a guinea and a half) could buy it piece by piece, and publishers could recoup their costs gradually. Advertisements bound into each installment furnished additional revenue.
Serialization also shaped the novels themselves. Because each part had to entice readers to return, authors learned to end installments with suspense or an unresolved question, and to sustain sprawling casts of idiosyncratic minor characters who could be revisited from month to month. Writing only a few installments ahead of publication, Dickens could respond to readers' reactions, and he occasionally altered his plans in response to letters or flagging sales. Critics have argued that the loose, episodic structure of many Victorian novels, sometimes disparaged as a defect, was a rational <u>adaptation</u> to the conditions under which they were written and read.
When I teach these novels, students are often astonished that the first readers waited a month for each new chapter. The experience of reading was also communal in a manner that is now scarce. A new installment could be discussed by families, read aloud to those who could not read, and debated in the press before the next appeared. Some commentators have likened it to following a television series week by week, and the comparison is apt — in both cases, the rhythm of release becomes part of the work's meaning.

Popular self-help literature often avers that imagining success vividly will help bring it about. The psychologist Gabriele Oettingen has spent decades scrutinizing that claim, and her findings suggest that it is, at best, partial. In a series of studies, people who indulged in especially positive fantasies about the future, Ⓐ<u>whether</u> about finding a job, recovering from surgery, or winning the affection of someone they admired, tended to fare worse than those whose expectations were more circumspect. Graduates who fantasized most glowingly about landing their ideal job (to take one example) submitted fewer applications and received fewer offers two years later.
Oettingen's explanation is that pleasant fantasies allow the mind to savor a goal as if it Ⓑ<u>had</u> already been achieved. In experiments measuring blood pressure, participants who wallowed in positive fantasies showed diminished signs of physiological energization, Ⓒ<u>suggesting</u> that the imagined success had partly sapped the motivation needed to pursue the real thing.
She does not conclude that people should abandon their dreams. Instead, she advocates a technique she calls mental contrasting. People first imagine the desired outcome and then deliberately identify the principal obstacle within themselves that stands in the way, such as a tendency to procrastinate or a fear of rejection. Juxtaposing the two images appears to fortify commitment to goals that are feasible and to help people disengage from goals that are not. Combined with specific plans for overcoming the obstacle, the method has been tested in studies Ⓓ<u>involved</u> students, patients, and employees, with encouraging results.
I have tried the technique myself before difficult deadlines, and the obstacle I identify is nearly always the same — my own procrastination. The research confounds a cultural message that equates optimism with success. Expectations, in Oettingen's account, are not the problem; people who judge their chances realistically and still expect to succeed tend to work hard. What erodes effort is fantasy that floats untethered from the reality it must eventually confront.

People from disparate cultures may, in some respects, literally perceive the world differently. A well-known experiment published in 2001 by the psychologists Takahiko Masuda and Richard Nisbett points in that direction. Japanese and American university students watched short animated scenes of an underwater environment featuring a few large, fast-moving fish together with smaller creatures, plants, rocks, and bubbles. Afterward, they were asked to describe what they had seen.
The American participants tended to commence with the most salient objects, typically by mentioning the big fish. The Japanese participants were more likely to begin with the setting, describing the water, the color of the background, or the plants, and they made more statements about relationships between the fish and their surroundings. In a subsequent recognition test, the Japanese participants were less accurate at identifying a previously seen fish when it appeared against an unfamiliar background, whereas the Americans' recognition was relatively unaffected by the change of context.
Nisbett and his colleagues interpret such findings as evidence of two broad cognitive styles.
