Analytic thinking (which they associate with Western societies) focuses on objects and their attributes, detaching them from their context. Holistic thinking (which they associate with East Asian societies) attends to the field as a whole and to the relations among its elements. They trace the difference partly to <u>divergent</u> social traditions, contrasting cultures that emphasize individual independence with those that emphasize interdependence.
The thesis has drawn trenchant criticism. Some researchers argue that the differences, although statistically reliable, are modest, that variation within each culture is substantial, and that labels such as Western and East Asian obscure immense heterogeneity. Others note that cognitive styles can shift with circumstance — people primed to think about relationships become more holistic, regardless of where they grew up. Even so, the studies have helped persuade psychologists that findings drawn from Western university students cannot automatically be assumed to describe human beings in general.

By the middle of the nineteenth century, Britain's factories were turning out furniture, textiles, and ornaments in unprecedented quantities, and many critics found the results deplorable. Machine-made goods, they complained, were shoddy in construction and smothered in imitative decoration, while the workers who produced them performed monotonous tasks that afforded no scope for skill or pleasure. The writer John Ruskin (1819–1900) argued that the degradation of the object and the degradation of the worker were inseparable, and his ideas made a profound impression on a young Oxford graduate named William Morris.
When Morris married in 1859, he and the architect Philip Webb designed a house for the couple, and finding nothing in the shops that satisfied him, Morris and his friends decorated it themselves. The experience led him in 1861 to found a firm that produced wallpapers, textiles, stained glass, and furniture by traditional methods. Morris immersed himself in obsolete techniques, reviving vegetable dyes and hand-block printing, and his flowing designs of intertwined leaves and birds remain familiar today. He insisted that people should keep nothing in their homes that they did not know to be useful or believe to be beautiful.
Morris's enterprise harbored a painful contradiction. Goods made slowly by skilled hands were expensive, and his customers were largely the affluent, whereas the ordinary workers he hoped to emancipate could not afford them. Morris was acutely conscious of this <u>predicament</u>, which helped draw him toward socialism in the 1880s; he came to believe that the conditions of labor could not be reformed without transforming society itself. In his final years he founded the Kelmscott Press (1891), producing exquisitely printed books.
The movement his example inspired took its name from the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society (founded in 1887), and it spread through Britain, Europe, and the United States. Its practitioners championed honest construction, respect for materials, and the dignity of handwork. Ironically, many of its ideals were eventually realized not by rejecting machines but by applying its principles of simplicity and integrity to industrial design — an outcome Morris himself might have regarded with ambivalence.

In most elections in the United States and Britain, voters mark a single candidate, and whoever receives the most votes wins, even without a majority. Critics maintain that this system (often called first past the post) yields skewed outcomes when more than two candidates compete. Voters who prefer a minor candidate may fear that supporting their favorite will merely help the candidate they like least — a dilemma known as the spoiler effect — and so they cast a tactical vote instead of a sincere one.
Ranked-choice voting (also called instant-runoff voting) is designed to address this problem. Voters rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first choices, the candidate with the fewest is eliminated, and the ballots of that candidate's supporters are transferred to their next preference. The process repeats until one candidate holds a majority of the remaining ballots. Australia has used a version of the system for elections to its House of Representatives for more than a century, and in recent years it has been adopted in the American state of Maine, for New York City's party primaries, and in Alaska.
Advocates claim that the method enables voters to express their genuine preferences without fear of wasting their votes, and that it encourages candidates to court the second-choice support of their rivals' voters, tempering campaign rhetoric. Detractors raise several objections. The ballots are more complicated, and some studies have found that a larger share of them are filled out incorrectly or exhausted, meaning that every candidate they rank has been eliminated before the final round. Counting can take longer, and results can be harder for the public to verify.
Political scientists also point out that ranked-choice voting is not immune to paradoxes. In rare cases, a candidate can lose by gaining support, or a candidate whom a majority prefers to every rival can be eliminated early. Such anomalies are by no means peculiar to this system; the economist Kenneth Arrow showed in 1951 that no ranked voting method can satisfy every reasonable criterion of fairness at once. The choice of an electoral system, in other words, is a choice among ____ rather than a quest for perfection.

Few aspects of schooling foment as much domestic strife as homework. Parents complain that it consumes family evenings; teachers worry that without it students will not practice enough; and students, for their part, rarely need persuading that there is too much of it. Surprisingly, the research evidence on its benefits is more equivocal than either its champions or its detractors tend to concede. As a parent, I have seen many evenings consumed this way at our own kitchen table.
The most influential reviews of the subject, conducted by the American psychologist Harris Cooper and his colleagues, found that the relationship between homework and achievement depends heavily on age. Among secondary school students, those who did more homework generally performed better on tests and in their grades, although the benefit appeared to level off beyond a certain amount. Among elementary school children, by contrast, the association was weak or negligible. Cooper has suggested a rough guideline of about ten minutes per night for each grade level (so that a child in the third grade would do about half an hour).
Interpreting such correlations is notoriously fraught. Students who do more homework may differ from their peers in motivation, parental support, or prior achievement, and struggling students may spend longer on assignments precisely because they find them hard. The quality of assignments matters too — tasks that ask students to practice skills already taught, or to apply them in unfamiliar contexts, appear more useful than busywork assigned out of habit.
Advocates of homework for young children argue that its value lies less in immediate academic gains than in cultivating habits such as time management and self-discipline, and in giving parents a window into what their children are learning. Skeptics retort that these benefits are largely unsubstantiated and that excessive assignments can breed rancor toward learning itself. The emerging consensus favors moderation — shorter, purposeful assignments in the early grades and more substantial work as students mature.

Like human languages, the songs of many birds vary from place to place. The phenomenon has been studied most closely in the white-crowned sparrow — a small songbird of North America. In the 1960s researchers in California discerned that males living only a few kilometers apart sang recognizably different versions of the species' song, with distinctive trills and phrases that marked each local population much as an accent marks a human speaker. On early walks I have noticed this myself — the sparrows in one park do not sound quite like those a few kilometers away.
Experiments illuminated how these dialects are acquired. Young males learn their songs by listening to adult males during a sensitive period early in life, then practicing, at first producing rambling, rudimentary sequences reminiscent of a human infant's babbling, before settling on a crystallized adult song. Birds raised in isolation sang abnormal songs, and birds exposed during the sensitive period to recordings of a particular dialect sang that dialect, even if it was not the one sung by their own parents. The song, in other words, is not fully encoded in the genes but must be learned from tutors.
Because the songs are learned, they are mutable. Researchers who compared recordings made decades apart in the San Francisco area found that some dialects had shifted over time, possibly in response to traffic noise (which masks lower frequencies and may favor songs pitched higher). A study of a related species, the white-throated sparrow in Canada, documented a new song variant that originated in the western part of its range and spread eastward across the continent within roughly two decades, <u>supplanting</u> the older version in many areas.
These findings make songbirds a valuable model for studying vocal learning — a capacity shared by relatively few animals, among them humans, parrots, hummingbirds, whales, and bats. The striking parallels with human speech, from the babbling stage to the importance of early exposure, have encouraged neuroscientists to investigate whether similar brain mechanisms underlie both.

When Mount Vesuvius erupted in the year 79, it buried the Roman town of Herculaneum beneath deep layers of volcanic material. In the eighteenth century, excavators tunneling into a luxurious villa outside the town discovered a library of papyrus scrolls, the only intact library known to survive from the classical world. The searing heat of the eruption had carbonized the scrolls, turning them into fragile black cylinders that resembled lumps of charcoal. Attempts to unroll them, first by hand and later with ingenious machines, obliterated many and yielded only fragments, while hundreds remained unopened for more than two and a half centuries.
In recent decades scientists have tried to read the scrolls without unrolling them. The computer scientist Brent Seales and his colleagues developed methods of virtual unwrapping — high-resolution X-ray scans reveal the internal structure of a scroll, and software traces its tightly wound layers and flattens them digitally. A formidable obstacle remained, however. The ink used at Herculaneum was carbon-based, and in the scans it is scarcely distinguishable from the carbonized papyrus on which it lies.
In 2023 a competition called the Vesuvius Challenge offered prizes to anyone who could extract legible text from the scans. Participants trained machine-learning models to detect subtle traces of ink, and in October of that year the first word to be read from inside an unopened scroll was announced — a Greek word meaning purple. In early 2024 a team of three students was awarded the grand prize for revealing several columns of text (apparently a work by an Epicurean philosopher reflecting on pleasure).
Scholars hope that the techniques will eventually allow the entire collection to be read, and some speculate that further excavation of the villa, much of which remains buried, might uncover additional scrolls. The project has also become emblematic of a novel kind of collaboration, in which classicists, physicists, and amateur programmers around the world work together to retrieve texts long considered irretrievably lost.
